newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Troubles of Venezuelan airline VIASA turn political.
newsitem.headline: Troubles of Venezuelan airline VIASA turn political.

text.p: Anger over Venezuela's struggling national airline Viasa grew on Friday as ministers prepared for talks with the Spanish government in an attempt to save the partly Spanish-owned carrier from bankruptcy.
Venezuela's National Investment Fund, the government body in charge of privatisations, said its President Alberto Poletto would fly to Madrid on Sunday for talks.
Loss-making Viasa suspended all its flights on Thursday for at least two weeks, stranding hundreds of passengers.
Spanish national airline Iberia, which has a 45 percent share in Viasa, said the suspension was "prudent, given the airline's position" and hoped "negotiations would reach a happy end".
But Venezuelan Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff again blasted Iberia, calling Viasa's unfolding woes a "chronicle of a bankruptcy foretold."
The company's fortunes took a turn for the worse earlier this month when workers overwhelmingly rejected an emergency cost-cutting plan.

The stalled negotiations soured further on Wednesday when two high-ranking Iberia officials were detained by Venezuelan police as they tried to leave the country. Police freed the executives after Spain voiced diplomatic surprise.
"The search for solutions should be conducted in a climate of respect and ... under the principles of judicial security," Iberia said in a statement.
Iberia reiterated its readiness to resume talks with the Venezuelan government, which has a 40 percent share, to find ways to refloat the airline, which was founded in 1960.

Both Iberia and the Venezuelan government have repeatedly said they were unwilling to pump money into a company that registered a $30 million loss last year and has not made a profit since Iberia took over management in 1991.
Although Viasa carries debts totalling $144 million, workers said they may have found a possible investor through French investment house Banque Paribas.
But company officials were doubtful. "Where's that investor? I don't see anyone," Viasa President Jose Campins said on Friday.
